utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. May I have the appearances please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Appearing for the Prosecution, Joanna Korner, Belinda Pidwell, and Crispian Smith on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing on behalf of Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic, Dragan Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is -- there is a preliminary matter that I wish to raise, and I discuss with the Ms. Korner, she has a preliminary matter. But since mine refers to yesterday's transcript, I kindly ask her for permission to state my preliminary matter first, and if it pleases the Court I may do so before the usher enters the witness in the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, before we hear from either counsel, there are two matters which the Chamber would raise. One is the long anticipated ruling on adjudicated facts. This, as counsel would appreciate, is an exercise which has consumed quite a bit of time out of court on behalf of the Chamber and its staff, and in order to bring this to as speedy a conclusion as possible, the Chamber has reluctantly decided that the better course would be to set aside a week, in order to deal with this. And it proposes - and this is largely a matter for the Office of the Prosecution, in terms of its own witness schedule, either the week beginning 8th February or the week beginning 15th of February, when it would set aside that time as out of court time in order to bring -- to complete its work on this matter. So if counsel -- if counsel, especially the Prosecution, would consider that proposal and inform us as soon as they're in a position to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can tell you straight away about the 8th of February; that's not possible. The witness who is coming is the one whom special arrangements have to be made for. Of safe conduct. I wasn't going to raise that. So that is not even a remote possibility. Your Honours, I had thought -- I have to say, that I thought the extra week in January had dealt with this. But I understand that there is some suggestion that the week after Easter was going to be one that was taken for consideration of outstanding motions. And although it's late, we have got witnesses lined up through -- I think we sent to the legal officers a list of all the witnesses we had lined up through February. I'm not saying that the week of --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. All -- I'm just being confirmed from Ms. Pidwell who has been dealing with this, that all witnesses to the end of February have been confirmed. Now, of course, we can unconfirm or try and unconfirm some of them, not that there is such a word in the English language. But it does cause, can I put it this way, some upset on behalf of the witnesses when they're told they are coming in a particular week, and then they are told, Forget it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We'll continue to look at it, Ms. Korner. But, of course, one of the factors that we take into consideration is that some of the witnesses who you have yet to call, what you do is dependant on the Chamber's ruling on that motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, yes. Yes and no. It is more a question of the -- what -- what the Chamber rules on adjudicated facts, in particular in relation to whether they apply to Zupljanin will affect not so much what we ask witnesses who are to come, but we may have to add witnesses. That's the problem. And I appreciate we have been asking the Chamber for some time to deal with this matter. It's just that we didn't appreciate that you were going to say that -- that you wanted a week. As I say, it's not -- it's not without possibilities to do the second week, but I'm told by Ms. Pidwell that the first week in March would be preferable because we haven't actually confirmed anybody yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: After you would have had time to consider it, you can let us know, and we'll take a final decision on the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, all I can say is it's -- certainly the week of the 8th of February is not an option.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yeah, we thought that that would have been the result, yes. We --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] The second matter is the ruling on yesterday's -- sorry. The second matter is the ruling on yesterday's motion by the Prosecution which parties would have had sight of by an advance courtesy e-mail. And the ruling is to the fact that yesterday the Prosecution informed the Chamber and the parties that it intends to use 55 intercepts with the Witness Zepinic, thus raising again the issue of admissibility of intercepts. The intercepts are listed and an e-mail message circulated late yesterday. Having considered the arguments of the parties present yesterday and taking into account both the jurisprudence of the Tribunal and the decision of this Chamber on the 16th of December of last year, the Trial Chamber's determination is as follows. The Trial Chamber bears in mind, that in order to be admissible in these proceedings and as set out in paragraph 14 of the decision of the 16th of December, any proposed exhibit, including an intercept, must be sufficiently reliable, authentic, and relevant to the proceedings in question. All those intercepts that meet all three criteria can be admitted. In the direction of the 16th December, the Trial Chamber has already found that intercepts are not, prima facie inadmissible on the grounds of illegality, and it has always been conceded by the parties and accepted by the Chamber that where a witness is able to identify his or her own voice on an intercept, and absent conflicting evidence, the relevant intercept may be sufficiently authenticated. The Chamber is satisfied that the witness can only satisfy the requirements of Rule 89, in respect of those intercepts where he was either, A, a participate in the discussion; or, B, physically present when the conversation took place, in which case he can only address the statements made by the person in who is presence he was at that time. This will require the witness to confirm in court that it is his voice on the intercept or that it is a conversation at which he was present. The Trial Chamber accepts that this witness may be able to provide information as to the relevance and context of matters discussed in other intercepts, and those may be put to the witness. However, following the reasoning set out above, any such intercept will remain marked for identification, unless the intercept has already been admitted in these proceedings. This also follows the past practice with the witness Branko Djeric. Therefore, the Trial Chamber will permit the Prosecution to seek admission through the witness Zepinic of only those intercepts for which he -- it is stated that he is a party to the conversation or during which he was present. The Trial Chamber has examined the list, and provisionally identified 15 such intercepts. However, the parties are free to bring to the attention of the Chamber any other intercepts that fulfil the criteria. As this -- as -- this ruling flows directly from the reasoning of our decision of 16th December. The Prosecution had the opportunity to take this into account when estimating the time available for this witness, and so there is no need to increase the time allotted for direct examination beyond the four hours already indicated. The Trial Chamber reiterates that the accused has the right to remain silent, but notes that as stated in paragraph 19 of 16th of December decision, the Defence must weigh the consequences of remaining silent and only presenting alternative evidence against using the opportunity to contradict the Prosecution evidence. The following is the list of the intercepts identified by the Trial Chamber stated by group -- group 1 number. And you may take the numbers as read. The following intercepts do not have a group number and are identified by a CD 1, number. And you may take those as read. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have matters to raise as a result of this ruling which was kindly notified to us in advance. But I will allow Mr. Zecevic first to deal with his matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, [In English] Your Honours, I will speak in English because I note I was, for the purpose of hearing Your Honours' ruling in Serbian, I put the -- the headphones off, and I don't believe that half of -- of very important part which you cite in your decision has been translated to Serbian. I'm really sorry to raise the attention to this. It is probably because of the -- the -- the manner of the speech or the -- or the fastness that Your Honour has given the decision. But I don't think that the -- that the interpreters were able to translate this in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I apologise for that. The -- would it assist that the -- that if a written decision is issued or the transcript is made available immediately?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as for myself, I don't have a problem. But I think maybe in due time if -- if this decision can be -- can be translated in B/C/S, it would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, either -- it was an oral decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And a written version of that oral decision can certainly be translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If that is the more efficient way of dealing with it, whatever. But I appreciate the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, there is -- well, one unfortunate matter that I have to raise concerning yesterday's transcript. Yesterday morning when we received the list of -- of our friends from the Prosecution with 391 documents which they offered -- which they proposed to offer to be admitted as the footnotes to Mr. Nielsen's report, Dr. Nielsen's report, I discussed before court with Mr. Thomas Hannis, and I -- I informed him that I would give him our position, the Defence position in the course of the day, because he -- he appreciated that 391 document we have to check, whether 65 ter list or we have other objections to that. Now, Your Honour -- Your Honours have ruled on page 68 and 69, line 1 to 8 on the admission of these documents, which -- which Mr. Hannis proposed. I -- I myself completely omitted that part of the transcript. It is probably due because I was getting ready for -- for the submission that was coming after, and I completely omitted, and I am deeply -- I deeply regret that. But, Your Honour, we do have an objection to that. I know it's -- it's post-festum that I'm raising this, but if you permit me to explain, I believe you will understand why it is our position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honours, the essence of our objection refers to 24 documents which are the intercepts listed in the footnotes to Nielsen report. Now, if these documents are admitted, we would be, at the very same time when Your Honours rule today and in light of your 16 December decision, we would basically have two different standards for the similar documents. It is only logical that Mr. Nielsen was neither party to one of the conversation or was physically present during that conversation. And for that reason, these intercepts should be treated like the -- the -- all other intercepts which you took the position on, in -- in your ruling of 16th of December and today. Therefore, there is these 24, 65 ter documents, the footnotes to Mr. Nielsen's report, that we object to be its admission. Those are the intercepts. I can provide the numbers, if -- if it pleases the Court, or I can provide the numbers by e-mail to -- to all parties, in order to save time on the -- on the transcript. I am again very sorry to bring it today, but it is entirely my mistake, and I'm -- and I am -- I'm regretful for that. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Of course, to the extent that there is fault, and what you're pointing out is the Chamber by admitting those documents acted inconsistently with its own ruling of the 16th December, reiterated subsequently that it is something to which the Chamber itself should have been alive. But let me hear what the other side has to say in response.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually, this is all part of and parcel what I wanted to raise with Your Honours as a result of the ruling. Firstly can I also point out - it may not be that the Defence have looked at it - that Your Honours have also admitted intercepts as part of the 92 ter package that is going along with the witness who is coming. I've forgotten his number, but the one who requires safe conduct. So there are, I am afraid, a number of inconsistencies in how these documents have been treated. But can I -- can I say why I think it -- in one sense it is right. First, the intercepts which a part of the package have been admitted in at least the other case in which the transcript forms part of the 92 ter package, and in this particular witness's case, these particular intercepts have been admitted in a number of other cases. Your Honours' ruling seems to suggest - and this is what really I'm seeking clarification - first, that, the next witness will have to listen in front of His Honour -- in front of Your Honours to his voice and tape and identify it, having already done so yesterday, as I explained, with the investigator and on the schedule. Now that in itself is going to take a little time. Second, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, if I may interrupt before you go further along that line, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We don't follow why that is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because that's what you say. You say this will require the witness to confirm in court that it is his voice on the intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, but he would have done that in the course of preparing the -- in the course of his being prepared, and the result of that being summarising in the spreadsheet, he would have done so. And when we deal with the intercepts item by item, he can say whether this is one in which he recognises his voice or whether he was present. I don't see how -- how the question of him having to listen to these transcripts in court arises.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, Your Honour, that's how we read that. But in any event, I don't think it will be as simple as that because the witness -- if we say intercept 65 ter number 1056 on the 21st of April, and you listen to it, can you confirm that's your voice. He didn't have transcripts. He was deliberately not given transcripts, Your Honour, because we wanted him to listen to -- to the voices. So it is not that he had a transcript in front of him saying this is the witness and this is the person to whom he is talking. But can I move on from that. I'm grateful for that, although we may have to try and work out how we're going to do that without him listen doing it. But it seems to follow also that Your Honours are saying that admissibility of the intercepts depends on somebody who is a party to the conversation and/or present at the conversation, even if is he not on the telephone line, attesting to this. Now, Your Honour, if that's right, obviously it increases the number of witnesses we have to call, who are not dead, who have to testify, That's my voice on the line. And the third thing is this. I'm not sure that all of Your Honours may appreciate this. The identification of voices on the intercepts as shown in the transcripts that Your Honour has seen was actually done by people working in Sarajevo for the organisation that taped these -- these conversations, who had quite often never met any of these people, and those identifications were being made through listening or an analysis of voice. Whereas what you have here, for example, is a witness who can say, I have known certain of the participants in these phone conversations and listened to them and spoken to them on the phone, even though it is not recorded, on a number of occasions. So, Your Honours, at the moment this is -- what is unclear is what it is we have to do to get these intercepts admitted. And, for example, you use the Branko Djeric example of his failure to recognise the voice, so you didn't admit it. This witness listened to those three, and in one of them can say, I recognise the voice of Branko Djeric. Now, Your Honours, are you saying that doesn't make it admissible? Because if so, what does make it admissible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, may I put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: When a party produces an intercept before the Chamber and provide a transcript or -- and a declaration from the - I don't know for any better word - the interceptor, that is to say, the person, the agent who sat somewhere and taped the conversation. That person would normally indicate that this was a conversation between Mr. A and Madam B, because the interceptor, the agent sitting with his listening gear, would know from which numbers the calls were made, and by virtue of that identification would normally be able to say that this is a conversation between Mr. A and Madam B. In the Tribunal's jurisprudence, that evidence has normally been sufficient to establish the identity of those who are on the line. I don't see why, at all, you need Mr. Zepinic to come in, in addition now, to confirm the identity of the persons who speak on these intercepts that you are putting to us. You -- in my view, it would be sufficient to produce the statement from the interceptor, the agent, and that would do. So the Chamber is at some loss in understanding just why we need Zepinic. Now the additional problem with Zepinic or anyone else is that to ask a third party to confirm the identity of the speakers merely by listening to the intercept seems to us to be simply too -- too unsatisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It would be too unreliable. So to have Zepinic confirm that Mr. Stanisic spoke to Mr. Karadzic, or whoever it might be, may be of assistance, but I certainly wouldn't rely on it, even if Mr. Zepinic is supposed to be able to recognise Mr. Stanisic's voice very well, because they were good friends, or whatever, they spoke often to each other. It is simply not sufficiently reliable, especially when you have the normal option which is available to us. So that's we say that if you want Zepinic to confirm the identity of the speakers on these intercepts, then at least we should restrict ourselves to the intercepts in which Mr. Zepinic himself was one of the speakers. And if then he had -- merely an order to meet the request from the Prosecution, if then also Mr. Zepinic could say that he was in the room at a particular time, and this time can be confirmed, when he heard Mr. A speaking to Madam B, and after the conversation, Mr. A confirmed to Zepinic that it was indeed Mrs. B that he spoke to, and we can then, by verification of the time, conclude that this was indeed a conversation that took place between Mr. A and Madam B, then we would go along with that. But that's as far as we can go.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I -- I fully appreciate that. And, Your Honour, one of the matters that we have been discussing is whether we should move up the witness who is going to deal with the intercepts to a much closer stage to where we are now to deal with this. But, Your Honour, my understanding is that there is a wholesale out and out challenge, as you gathered from Mr. Zecevic and Mr. Pantelic yesterday, to not only, whether these intercepts are legal or illegal, whether they have been in some way doctored, but also to the voices on them. There is no admission. The Defence declined to make the admission. And, therefore, it seemed to us, sensible in the light of what we now know to be the Defence position, that in addition to the man who dealt with the intercepting, the interceptor who will say, Either this comes from this telephone number or from listening to this voice on countless occasions - which is part of the evidence as Your Honour Judge Harhoff knows - I can say this is X, to have some confirmation from someone who can say, I recognise the voice. It is not identification. It is recognition, which is different. Because I dealt with, for example, Mico Stanisic over a period of three years on a daily basis. And than is the reason. Now if Your Honours -- if what Your Honour is saying is, We will take -- we will admit the intercepts once we have heard the evidence from the people in Sarajevo, then, Your Honour, I certainly won't take up -- waste any time. But Your Honours are faced with what you heard yesterday from the Defence, and that is why I made this application. I hope that is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, the last point you made when you say the people in Sarajevo, you're talking about the persons who -- the technical persons who would have made the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, well, who are not, I may say, on our witness list at the moment. We have simply got the man -- overall charge. But they have been called in other trials. And it we're put to this challenge, we can call the various technicians. But at the moment, they're not on our witness list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... bring something else to your attention. Mr. Smith has looked up the witness from Sarajevo. He was a 92 ter package, and it looks, we're just checking, that Your Honours have already admitted all the intercepts. Or -- not all, but we're just checking. But the ones that were on ... Which makes life even more interesting.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There's a live mike on, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We thank counsel for their observations, but we don't consider it necessary to say anything beyond the ruling that we have delivered on these matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] The first 12 intercepts on -- The first 12 intercepts on our list were part of the package. And, at the moment, appear to be in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Which witness are we talking about, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think he is a protected witness, Your Honour. He is a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay, then give him a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I think the practice is that these parts of the package are not finally admitted until the witness has been heard. ST-108 hasn't been heard yet, so it's not finally admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, this may be a -- this is -- may be a side one, we'll have to sort that out later. I thought Your Honours admitted in lock, stock, and barrel. I didn't remember there being the caveat that only after he has given evidence. But anyhow, Your Honours, then can I return to how I deal with this. Your Honours is saying - are saying, sorry, is - are saying I can go into the content of some of the intercepts about which he may be expected to know something, particularly where his name is mentioned, but I should not ask him to say whether having listened to these intercepts he is able to identify the voice of the person he worked with for three years. I just want to understand that. Is that right, Your Honours? Because that seems to what your ruling seems to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We're speaking about several things at the same time, it appears. The issue of authenticity is a part of the process of admitting the intercept into evidence but is only one part. There's also the issue of relevance, and there's the issue of reliability. Now, only for the purpose of authenticity for that purpose only, I think Mr. Zecevic's testimony [sic] as to who is speaking is insufficient, unless he, himself, is a part of the conversation. You may put it to him for contents or for other purposes. But for the authenticity, we would require more solid evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, that's all I'm asking. So I can't say to him, Have a look at what is said to be an intercept of a conversation of Mico Stanisic and Radovan Karadzic, did you recognise the voice? Yes, Mico Stanisic. I now want to ask you about some of the content about which you may be expected to be able to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I think you can [Realtime transcript read in error "can't"] ask him whether he recognises or not. But you can't ask as a result of that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: To admit it as --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you, Your Honours, yes, that's the first matter. The second matter is this: Your Honours say I can't have more than four hours and say that we should have thought about it when we got your ruling. Your Honour we give the estimate of four hours before we got the ruling about the admission of intercepts. Then when we put together the package of what he would -- to listen to, it was then that we appreciated that there were a large number about which he could make informed comment. If Your Honours limit me to the four hours, then I cannot ask the witness to assist us on quite a lot of these intercepts. So that's -- because you say we should have known about it once we got the ruling, but the estimate of four hours was given before, was given in November. So I'm in Your Honours hands on this, but clearly to be able to deal with it, I need more than four hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you should begin, and at the end of that four hours, we would consider your application for further time then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, Your Honour, it's page 16, line -- line 18 and 19. His Honour Judge Delvoie, I think he said something along these lines, I think you can ask him, if I'm right. So for the purposes of precision of transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you. So could the usher escort the witness to the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you sir. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir. You have now taken a solemn declaration as a witness before this Tribunal, and the -- I would begin by asking you your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Vito Zepinic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 27 of June, 1953.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am doctor of medicine, Ph.D. degree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Australian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Australian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You have not testified previously before this Tribunal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, the procedure is that the side calling you - in this case, the Prosecution - would begin by asking you questions, and then counsel for each of the accused would have a right to put questions to you, after which the Prosecution may have further questions arising out of such questions, as were put on behalf of the accused, and the Chamber may, itself, have questions by way of clarification. And upon the completion of that exercise, you would be released as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Zepinic, the learned Judge asked you what ethnicity you were, and you said Australian. Before you became an Australian were you a citizen of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And under which ethnic grouping would you have come -- did you come?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I always indicated myself as a Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So for the purposes of any census or elections you called yourself a Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to ask you a little bit more about your background. I think that you finished medical high school and then went to the University of Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And after had you obtained your bachelor of medicine qualification did you go to Belgrade University and obtain a master's degree?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I finish the master degree in medicine in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And thereafter did you complete your PhD in 1985?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I'm not quite sure, 1984 or 1985, doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: For anyone who wants to have look at it, I think your Ph.D. is filed at Belgrade University. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you practice in general medicine for some years in Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Only shortly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then were you employed by the corrective services in the Department of Justice dealing effectively with delinquents?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: It was my interest regarding further post graduate study because both thesis master degree, and Ph.D. degree, I finished in field of forensic psychiatry, in particularly regarding research in delinquency.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Was it during this period that you first met Momcilo Mandic?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I think so. I would say that we met during his time when he was a judge in court in Sarajevo. And I think that for the first time we met during my -- doing a job as a court expert, a court witness about my field.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I think it is also right that you were awarded a Fulbright scholarship to study in Chicago.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did a project regarding investigation in the field of delinquency, in adolescent delinquency in Chicago, but I didn't have such pleasure and opportunity to being achieved and to go there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: To put matters fairly shortly because this is all background, I think the communist party made allegations that you were supported by the CIA, and were you then expelled from the communist party?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: That was -- I would say common with young people who wanted to further study abroad, and my interest was science. I honestly speaking cannot recall on which basis communist party made such decision and on which information they stated that I am connected with CIA or any other organisation or association in America instead of being interested in particular and specifically about my science and my professional field.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then I think eventually to lead into your career with the police, did you obtain, in 1986, employment as director of the police academy in Vrace?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was appointed as -- under Vrace police academy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you a lecturer in the Faculty of Medicine in the University of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I was associate, I would say lecturer in the University of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, after the elections in 1990 -- let's start before the elections. Did you join any of the nationalist parties?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: No. Not national, but also nor any other party, because during election after crash, I would say, of communist party in early January 1990s, it was established many other parties in Bosnia and other states in former Yugoslavia, but I didn't join any party. Not national, but no other party as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. After the elections, were you nominated by the SDS for the position of minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, please, how it come about that the SDS nominated you for this position.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Well, I was approached, I would say, by a few of my good friends, all nationalities, because during, I would say, election and during promotion of national parties, it was obvious that national parties have something which is not, I would say, promising as a unity of my former country. And I had already, I would say, reputation as a liberalist who is looking about, you know, qualities not about national -- national basis, and I was approached with -- to accept some nomination, in particular in interior ministry because of my previous experience because of my reputation, because of my connection with many people being my students in police academy, and in particular, also, because of my professional research that I did in delinquency. So I would say that now any national leader directly approached to me asking me for appointment, it was rather, I would say, my friends who asked me to accept some position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Did you have a meeting with anybody from the SDS about your accepting the nomination for this position?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was invited to attend at a meeting -- headquarter of SDS, Djuro Djakovic in Sarajevo with a friend of mine Miodrag Simovic that I know him for long period of time. I met there with Dr. Karadzic. I think it was Momcilo Krajisnik. I can't recall other people being present. And I remember that they explained to me that, on the agreement between national parties that SDS should recommend somebody who will take role as a deputy minister. I should mention here nobody, including Dr. Karadzic or Momcilo Krajisnik, they didn't require any membership to the SDS, and I have never been member of SDS. Nobody required for that. I explained to them my concept, if I'm nominated. Dr. Karadzic was a little bit, you know, reluctant saying that probably my concept is not in accordance with some, you know, national parties concept. Mr. Krajisnik responded in way like, We expect that you a good man, that you will do your job professionally, and that you are not going to move into any -- anybody's favour. That was very short meeting with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, had you met either Dr. Karadzic or Mr. Krajisnik before this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So, on that basis, did you accept the nomination for deputy minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: It wasn't meeting to accept a role. It was meeting to explain that I'm ready to, you know, to take that position. In particular, that national parties, SDS and SDA, had the long discussion meetings regarding which nationality should take control over interior ministry, probably reasonable considering that it was only, I would say, armed force in our state. In -- I remember that Muhammed Cengic was very keen to take role as interior ministry. SDS was against. And apparently they tried to find somebody who is in between.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Can I just ask what you -- you said a moment ago, that the -- there were long discussions about who could control the interior ministry. Because it was, you would say, the only armed force in your state. Why do you say that, given that there was the JNA as well at the stage?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: JNA was under command of federal institution, not on the state constitution. And also we have Territorial Defence which was also on the command of JNA, so practically speaking, state has interior ministry, the police, and reserve police that state can use in case of some, you know, necessary issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. In any event, did you obtain, were you appointed to the position of deputy minister of the interior at the assembly held in February 1991?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Beg your pardon, can you repeat your question and translation. Because it is distracting, your question and translation, if you don't mind, I will listen. If necessary I will ask Your Honour to translate something if I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you're happier to speak in English, and if you don't understand something then you will use the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Because it is quite distracting listening, you know, question, and listening to translation at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The question I asked was this: Were you in fact appointed to the position of the deputy minister of the interior by the assembly held in February of 1991?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And at the same time was Alija [overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... appointed as a minister, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was appointed the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers kindly not overlap for the sake of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now I'm doing what normally is the problem here, that two people speaking English go at speed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like you to have a look, please, at a diagram which was attached to our pre-trial brief and is -- it's exhibit -- ir 65 ter 10138.4.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Korner, the previous question of yours and the comment by the witness didn't enter -- wasn't entered into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you said, yes. At the same time, was the question, that Alija Delimustafic was appointed minister, and you said yes.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The diagram, Your Honours, is page 4 in the bundle that Your Honours all have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I think, Mr. Zepinic, you had a chance to look at this earlier.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Any comments you want to make about the -- the format of this?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I would make two comments here. I don't think that we have assistant secretary for - I can't read - public security that Jusuf Pusina was appointed on that position. I think he was director of police academy. And Mr. Stanisic was appointed as an advisor to cabinet of ministry, minister and with other two advisors as well. So, you know, putting his position right now here, it seems that he had higher position than under-secretary of security service, or higher position than any assistant, in particular department. I don't think that we should put on him such position that he didn't help.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you would say the position of advisor to the secretary which Mr. Stanisic became in 1992, is one that is what, on a level with an under-secretary?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And you think that Mr. Pusina was the director of the school?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Otherwise, does this diagram accurately represent the people who were in these positions during this period?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I think so. Except on the -- our documents that chief of security in Sarajevo was a member of our cabinet. And Mr. Stanisic was previously appointed as a chief of CSB Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now you have -- thank you very much. You've talked about our cabinet. Can you tell us what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I mean cabinet of ministry. Minister that includes our assistants in different areas, like, crime, information, finances and police. Uniformed police. And also secret service with under-secretary as a member of our cabinet. And he has also two his assistants regarding his role. And, again, in case that we needed something regarding in general the state in our cabinet meetings, we invited chiefs of regional security police services, CSB like Mr. Zupljanin from Banja Luka, or any -- any other -- or centre. We had on that time, if I remember well, ten centres in the state.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I think you will find that it was nine which are shown here.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Bihac, Banja Luka, Livno, Doboj, Tuzla, Zenica, Sarajevo, Gorazde, Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now I can move straight away, because you have mentioned both of them, to your knowledge of, first of all, Mico Stanisic. When did you first meet him?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Honestly speaking, I cannot recall for the first time. I really can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. If we could place it -- had you met him before the 1990 elections?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I would say yes considering that he was a member of judo club and I was president of karate club. It's two sports we never, you know, liked each other. It's a clash all the time. So apparently I saw him before and met him before, but not establishing any particular friendship.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: After your appointment as deputy minister, how often would you see or have dealings with Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I didn't have a meeting with Mico Stanisic until his appointment as chief of Sarajevo CSB.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And once he had been appointed, how often would you have meetings with him or see him after that?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Well, depends of problems that we discussed regarding Sarajevo region. Again, he was on few occasions invited in our cabinet meeting regarding that. Depends, I can't say we -- we met once a week or twice per day, or we had, you know, conversation on daily basis. Depends which problem arise in Sarajevo that I can -- or needed to contact him and resolve the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, what about Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Stojan Zupljanin was previously appointed as a chief of centre in Banja Luka. He was a well-experienced policeman. If I remember well, he finished law in Sarajevo and then being appointed as a crime inspector in CSB Banja Luka, and was upgraded to commander in some station, and until being appointed as a chief of CSB Banja Luka. So we accepted his position. We didn't replace him after we -- being appointed. And it was his duty as a chief of CSB Banja Luka to send us any information regarding security out of that particular region. Again, if something that would be discussed on the state level, he would be invited to attend to our cabinet meeting, together with his usually under-secretary of security service.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And roughly how often do you think you would see him or speak to him?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't say exactly. If I can say, maybe -- if I remember well, we had meetings, maybe four, five times in the cabinet meeting, inviting him as a chief of CSB Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you ever go to Banja Luka --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes I had on many occasions some problems that I needed to be there. And my first visit in Banja Luka region was a couple of days after being appointed because of problem in Bosanski Dubica between Croatia and citizens, I would say, who lived in Bosnia and citizens who lived in -- in Croatia. It was very close between Kutina, if my memory is still very well. It is kids who attended primary school attended in the [indiscernible] Sava river because it was closer than going to Dubica. And at the same time, the high school kids from Croatia visited and attended at Bosanska Dubica. It was quite common in Bosnia, like Bosanski, Slovanski Brod, Bosanski -- anyway -- so but unfortunately --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I -- I'm sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: That's fine, no problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is simply that we have limited amount of time. I was just trying to get at how often you had, you know, been to Banja Luka, so you had met with Zupljanin, that's all.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I can't exactly number. But any time when I needed something or -- or if situation required from me to be there, considering my position, it was quite normal to invite and have a meeting with chief of, you know, CSB to discuss about issue. Sorry. We had a, I would say, common -- and as war erupted in Croatia, I would say that we had more frequent meetings in the end of 1991 than in the beginning of 1991, because, simply of security reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to have to go back for a moment, but I think because we have been slightly talking over each other, that the shorthand writer, it doesn't appear what you said about Stanisic. That's at page 26, line 6. You said the chief of security in Sarajevo was a member of our cabinet and Mr. Stanisic was previously appointed as chief of ...

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Sarajevo centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... SUP.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes, before being appointed as an advisor to ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Doing it again. Right. Thank you very much. Now, could we move, please, to the reporting procedures and what information was given to you as deputy minister and to the minister himself. We see you had -- there were a number of assistant secretaries. Would they deliver reports to you or to the minister? And, if so, how often?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: From whom?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: From the various assistant secretaries for the prevention and detection of crime which was Momcilo Mandic.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Oh yes, it was their duty as our assistants to provide us necessary information regarding, I would say, general issues. But assistants had also responsibility for own department, to act and take action in accordance with our internal documents. In particular, we discuss about report provided to us, what is related with state not the particular, I would say region, or particular CSB. If necessary, assistant can report us about something that we can discuss such issue on the cabinet meeting as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Can we deal with looking at it -- can we look at it from the hierarchy point of view. Would the SJBs have to deliver reports to the CSBs within their area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Can you say again, please, your question, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. What I'm calling the SJBs --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- would they have to give regular reports or reports to the CSBs?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think that you are confusing me talking about the same body.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Can we have up the -- the chart again please.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes. CSB.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We see the CSBs there?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And underneath them are shown, for example, if we take --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: SJB.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: That's police station.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are kindly asked not to overlap.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... every police station should be informed chief of CSB. So CSB as a chief from the region should inform us what is going on -- on particular area. So as you see, for example, in Banja Luka, see here, we have Banja Luka CSB and we have many other SJB. It is [B/C/S spoken]. So they had a commander who is responsible and to inform CSB if necessary if something urgent, a copy of or any information should be sent to us directly in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. What -- what would you call something urgent that required immediate reporting to the ministry?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: In wasting time, for example, if something occurred, like, catastrophe or terrorist attack or they captured somebody dealing with drugs or money smuggling or whatever, if necessary, if CSB was unable to take control or deal with a current problem, SJB can request directly from ministry to support in taking action.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We have seen from other evidence that there was -- there -- subsequent to the period, however, when the Republika Srpska, the Serbian Republic was established, that SJBs were sending or were told to send weekly reports to the CSBs. Would those reports sent to the CSBs be also copied and sent up to the ministry?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes. The station, police station in particular region sent -- it was normal, I would say, daily reporting what is going on in the field, and CSB had everyone had information, you know, unit to provide necessary information to send to ministry directly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now, what sort of reporting went on between the minister of the interior and the Presidency, for example?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: By the law we had obligation to inform, I would say, governments, parliaments and Presidency about situation on daily basis, providing bulletins, gazettes, or other paper. And it was common that we not only sending written information, attending meetings, informing Presidency or parliament - and government was, you know, part of our regular meetings - or being invited by a member of Presidency or president of Presidency to give some brief regarding situation on the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to move, please, to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, if you are about to move to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I have just been handed a note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You're just a few seconds short of the usual time for the adjournment. So we rise for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is coming back into court, it just occurred to us a number of witnesses had talked in relation to these charts we produced for the pre-trial brief. I wonder if i could just have the book, as it were, exhibited now so that we have an exhibit number for it. It's 65 ter 10138. And then we can have point 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5. I don't know why it thought it was already in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So did I, until it was suddenly pointed out that it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honors, we do have some objections in that respect because we don't think that that's completely accurate. But we can deal with that through cross-examination. But what I was -- what I had in -- in mind also was that maybe we divide because each and every page is a different chart. So maybe it can be -- let's say, 100.1, 2, 3, 4, and so and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In order that will give us a much better view of the exhibit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we certainly agree to that. We think that's sensible. And as I say, and obviously witnesses are making slight corrections. Can I put it this way, it is admitted as an exhibit, errors and omissions to be rectified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... so admitted and marked, errors and omissions excepted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P873, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Maybe not what Your Honours said, but it may be the reality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: For the transcript it should read, errors and omissions accepted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: A, double C, and not e-x-c-e-p-t.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, Mr. Zepinic, that was a slight digression. I said I was going to move to a different topic, and I would like to ask you please about the principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. Due to this the number wasn't entered. The P number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for the sake of transcript, the number is P873.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Point so-and-so, as the -- according to the different pages and the different charts in the book. The Registry will indicate the particular numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Moving now to a slightly different more general topic, if we may. I want to ask you please to tell the Court about your understanding of the principle of resubordination of the police to the army, appreciating that you are talking about the period when you were Assistant Minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry. Before the witness answers that, perhaps I shouldn't have inserted that English expression excepted. It now reads accepted. The word should have been excepted. E-x-c-e-p-t-e-d. Not accepted, excepted. We all understand what it means, that subject to the errors and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Zepinic, resubordination, please, if you could tell the Court your understanding of this principle.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: My understanding, first of all, you should understand that JNA of Yugoslav People's Army was under control of federal Presidency. Previously chief commander was president of Yugoslavia. And after Tito died, it was Federal Presidency as a chief of army. It was prime minister cabinet, having member of Ministry of Defence. At the same time, it was chief in general, General Kadijevic on time when we are talking about 1990 and 1991. By federal -- I'm not lawyer by my occupation, and I apologise many lawyers in this room, better will, I will say, explain regarding legal issues. But army was under control of the federal institution, JNA. We had in any state, in every state, territorial army as a part of army force that should be, if necessary, under command of JNA. By law on that time constitution, state and federal, we have three levels of implementation or subordination between army, JNA, and police force in any state. In case of crisis in some state, police is responsible directly to state Presidency, and state Presidency should make decision about involvement, and if necessary, on ministry request, approval to engage reservists in state to look after something what is necessary for security reasons. In case of imminent war threat, police, in any state, with decision made by federal Presidency can be under command of JNA, in some particular region to resolving problem like, you know, terrorists being in particular or anything else that has happened. And in case of war situation, army practically is taking control over all forces in any -- any state. I'm talking about what's happened in former Yugoslavia before disintegration practically of former Yugoslavia and before the federal Yugoslavia, republic of Yugoslavia, was disintegrated into independent countries starting from Slovenia, Croatia and later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: So that was subordination between army and police. In case that, again, the necessary, federal Presidency could make decision to engage, for example, Special Police force unit from my state Bosnia and Herzegovina to be involved or any police -- policeman to be involved in some crisis region in former Yugoslavia to support peace and establishing, you know, law and order. What's happened, for example, in 1981 [sic], in Kosovo crisis when first erupted. On that time federal Presidency established, I would say, a federal committee for Kosovo involving all policemen form state republics under federal control and federal order that was under federal ministry command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that in the case of a war situation, the army practically took control over all forces. When you talk about a war situation, could that be one that just came about, or did there have to be a declaration of war made?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Federal Presidency, as a chief of army, and, you know, highest ranking, I would say, body in our former country should announce war situation and give instructions to all states and all subjects being involved in dealing with war situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If there was an imminent threat of war, you say, again, would that require there to be some kind of a declaration?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes. In case of imminent threat of war, federal Presidency can make some declaration regarding involvement of police units under army [realtime transcript read in error "aerial"] control, but not necessarily all of them should be. In case, for example, that some crisis erupted, for example, in some region in former Yugoslavia, like the [indiscernible] Bosnia, whatever, federal Presidency will announce, you know, crisis situation, and that practically some part or all police -- policemen should be under army control and command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, you said that the federal Presidency could make a declaration regarding the involvement of police units under army - as opposed to aerial command - but would the president -- the federal Presidency have to declare that an imminent state of war or threat of war existed?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. If there was simply the declaration that an imminent threat of war existed, who would be responsible for the disciplining of police?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Who is commanding them. If they implemented in armies action they had responsibility practically on the army role because no one policeman can be employed as a policeman before serving compulsory military service in former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So if they were ordered to serve in a -- in -- under the army, it was the army who was responsible for disciplining them?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If no such order existed, but the police, for example, were sent to assist the army in guarding prisoners, who be would be, in your understanding, responsible for disciplining --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: The ministry, our ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you say your ministry, the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Ministry of Interior, yes. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. That's all I want to ask you about that topic. You mentioned the Special Police. Can I ask you, please, about the Special Police. At the time when you were minister -- sorry, deputy minister.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Thank you for promotion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who was in charge of the Special Police?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Commander at that time was Dragan Vikic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And to whom did Mr. Vikic report?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Well, when he came under power, we changed previous rule, and did agreement between me and Alija Delimustafic that Special Police force cannot be used in any circumstances without both of us signing, agreeing, including commander of Special Police force. So nobody practically in my state, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, had rights legally to use or ask Special Police force to do something without our signature and our agreement. It was deliberately, to be honest, change rules, because we tried to prevent the eventuality of misusing Special Police which had, at that time, between 3 and 400 specially trained young people, fully equipped in case of something necessary to intervene. They had special accommodation, they lived there all the time, in Krtelji Sarajevo, and all the practically, in case that they don't do other duties, like guarding Presidency, parliament, or government. They had regular training every day regarding ability, incapability to take role, if necessary. Sorry for interrupting, I'm sorry. I deeply apologise to you. At the same time we had some, I would say, also young people that being as a Special Police force in regional CSBs. But on that -- on our time, chief of CSB couldn't use Special Police force from his region and his stations, police stations, without our agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That was actually the next thing I was going ask you. So there were in fact Special Police within the CSBs. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But in order for them to be used -- your permission -- sorry, I your, the ministry's permission had to be obtained?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes, our order practically would be order to use Special Police unit in some CSBs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, can I just ask the witness if Special Police force units existed even on the SJB level, on the lowest, the police station level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a Special Police unit in every CSB in regional areas. And they responsible practically to chief of CSB, but cannot be used or moved to do any activities without order from ministry directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. But my question was, just to be sure, if underneath the CSB, the police stations, the SJBs, would also have a small Special Police unit? Or did the Special Police unit only exist at the CSB level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I should explain something more precisely. In any CSB, SJB, some people being part of police station. SJB didn't have police unit but had some individuals as a part of Special Police unit that is part of CSB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So what you are saying is that the members of the Special Police unit which resorted under the CSB, those individual members would be scattered around in the police forces of the SJBs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pleasure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you were appointed in February 1991, and Mr. Delimustafic was appointed the minister. Were you given any sort of name by the press? Names, I should say.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yeah, look, I would say that we had very good relationship regarding dealing with our ministry, trying to oppose division of our ministry, trying to oppose any implementation on national basis or, you know, and somehow, somewhere, I don't -- I can't -- I cannot recall exactly time, press called us Boro and Ramiz. Who is Boro who is Ramiz, I don't know really, to be honest. It was symbolic from Second World War, two young fellows in south of Serbia gave, you know, everything possible to protect, you know, people around from fascists. So, yeah, they called us Ramiz and Boro, and I can't tell you who was who, Boro and Ramiz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was -- what were they trying to suggest by that?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Trying to suggest practically that we, being -- I wouldn't say it is very hard or maybe too optimistic saying that we being as a symbol of unity, in dealing in quite difficult time, resisting any -- anything what can disturb our policy, in keeping peace and unity of our minister as much as we could. That's probably -- was, I would say, motive for news reporter reporting something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to move on, then, to how things developed through 1991. But you told us that you first met Karadzic at this meeting before you were nominated. After your appointment, how often would you meet with -- or see Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I would say I -- I met with Dr. Karadzic less frequently than with other political leaders in Bosnia and Herzegovina, simply because he wasn't member of any governing body. He was only party leader. So it was probably less frequent that I had meeting Alija Izetbegovic or Kljuic or Biljana Plavsic or Mr. Krajisnik or Jure Pelivan. In case of something is necessary regarding SDS from security point of view, I would be invited to attend on the assembly affairs of theirs in case something is related concerning SDS as a party of coalition, we had a meeting or, you know, phone calls, you know. But, again, I would say he -- I had less frequently meeting with him than other political leader. He never attended our cabinet meeting. He never visited our building at all. Why, I don't know. Apart from other political leaders, you know, being quite present and coming to see us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In any of the meetings you had with him, did he express any views about the unity between Muslims and Serbs and Croats, as you have expressed you and Mr. Delimustafic were seen as a symbol of that unit. What was Dr. Karadzic's attitude to this?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I would regress a little bit, you know, back. I think that our national leaders, political leaders, Mr. Kljuic, Izetbegovic, and Karadzic, it was, I would say, message to people in Bosnia that they united on national basis to deal with situation in Bosnia, forming coalition. They told us with coalition, we can do, live, and act together. So what's ever happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina, they did together. They had a power. Apart from discussions of, you know, assemblies of national parties, attending of some assemblies, I never heard any political leader from national party saying, Yes, we can live together. But in case that they needed to keep a power as a coalition, they always being together. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm dealing specifically with Mr. Karadzic and any conversation --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I had many conversation with Dr. Karadzic regarding his view that, you know, that life together between three nationalities in -- in former Yugoslavia -- or Bosnia, pardon me, is impossible. It -- it was always saying what's happened in the past, you know. And I remember once we had a dinner at his flat, I would say, and he told me that, you know, what's happened during Second War, and something like that, and that it was civil war, and something like that, that it was wrong by Tito and communist party to establish former Yugoslavia, in particular in Bosnia three nationalities living together, considering, you know, civil conflict during Second World War. However, I mentioned to him that probably bloodiest civil war we had in USA by President Lincoln establishing own country without any problem and they living together, we know what is -- what has happened. So that was my -- my concept, actually, that people can live together if they have desire to live together with tolerance and with understanding, and respect to each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever mention to him your own family in connection with -- your family circumstances in connection with living --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I think that Dr. Karadzic also had in his extended family some other nationalities, not only Serbs but also Montenegrins. And I had also -- like everyone in -- in particularly in Bosnia, if we are saying that, if I remember well, around 60 per cent of families in former Bosnia being mixed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And in your family, was this also true?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes, my sister is married with a Muslim, and I ask him, Look, if Serbs and Muslims cannot live together, can you tell me on which way I will say to my sister that her husband is not good guy? So that's...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You mentioned also Biljana Plavsic. How often did you have dealings with her?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: As a -- as my role, I -- I attended on many occasions Presidency meetings, and she was also chairman of security committee of Presidency. That is -- my role was also to attend. So any Security Council meeting, I have to be present there, or anything on a Presidency, considering security issues, and safety issues, I was invited to be there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And from your dealings with her, what was her attitude towards, if you like, a multi-ethnic Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: It -- it was nearly, I would say, similar, what Dr. Karadzic explained it. Division on national basis is imminent and that apparently three nationalities cannot live in unity. That was my also, I would say, opposition saying, If we cannot live together, how you can govern this state together?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mico Stanisic, who you told us your dealings with him, was he a member of any political party, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I have no recollection that he was particular member of party. I met with him a few times on the SDS Assembly being invited because of, you know, topic that my ministry should answer or, you know, deal with. And I ask him, Why you are here? Considering that his role wasn't to represent ministry. And he told me, I am member of party. But I cannot give you clear evidence that he was a member of SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In any of your dealings with him, did he express any views to you about the Serbs and Croats and Muslims being able to live together?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I -- I can't remember. I don't -- I can't recall that he is particular saying that Muslims and Serbs and other nationalities, Croats, cannot live together. Mico usual would approach, like, that Serbs, under some, I would say, sideline about situation in -- in ministry or any other institution in -- in the state, in Bosnia, including some departments, including, you know, people being appointed or something like that. But I cannot say that he was hard-lined member of SDS saying, We cannot live with Muslims or Croats together.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, can I just go back over your answer because it has come out slightly oddly in the transcript. You said his -- his approach was something about the Serbs being sidelined in the ministry or ...

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Not only in -- in our ministry but in -- in other institutions as well. That was his -- his view.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: His view was that Serbs were being sidelined?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then I want to move, please, to some of the documents that reflect on the events of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we start, please, by having a look at a document, which is 65 ter number 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, if I may ask Ms. Korner. Mr. Cvijetic just informed me that again a part of -- of the exchanges between the witness and -- and Ms. Korner has not been translated in Serbian, so ... If I may ask Ms. Korner just -- and the witness just to pause between the -- the answer and the question -- the question and the answer, so as to give the opportunity to the interpreters to interpret that in -- in Serbian. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now this is a document which is headed, in English: Possibilities to decentralise internal affairs in Bosnia and Herzegovina. You looked at this document, I think, this morning. Had you seen it before?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Not by my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I should explain we discovered this morning when we were going through the documents that we have two English translations, and it's been pointed out to me that I appear to be working off a slightly different one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Zepinic. So you had not seen this before?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's an undated document. And when you -- are you able to assist at all with looking -- when you look at the contents, as to -- if you can give us a sort of rough date when it might have been drafted.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: No problem at all. I can assist you in making comments what is inside regarding contents of this document. But if I can make my comment before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know who made this document. It could be somebody's, you know, assumption. I don't think this is legal documents that came from my ministry, otherwise I would be well informed about it. Secondly, I don't know the dates of these documents, so if you are asking me to assist regarding contents about documents, I will assist you. But definitely I cannot accept this document as a valid document made from my ministry, or sent to my ministry by anyone, considering again that I don't know who is author of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I'm not suggesting it was an official document from your ministry. But from having read it, are you able to assist --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
