utterances.text: -- as to whether or not whoever wrote it, had knowledge of the -- how the police worked. Is that something that can you assist us on?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yeah, can I assist you in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. That was a question. Didn't sound like one; it was a question. Would the person who wrote this have to have had knowledge of the police?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Perhaps we can go to the second page of this in English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. It says: "Organisation and manner of conducting internal affairs in circumstances when social relations in the Republic are being decentralised has a great significance and role ..." And then if we go to the third paragraph: "In the assessment and evaluation of the necessity to decentralise relations in the Republic as an appropriate response to the disintegration processes in Yugoslavia." Does that help in -- in dating when this document was written, because, later on, we can see: "Decentralisation in internal affairs right now would play into the hands of the Croatian successionists." So does that help you?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Some nationalists in former Yugoslavia had, you know, Serbian or Croatian expanse units or nationalists for nearly five decades. So I, honestly speaking, don't see any value of this document, and this is somebody's, I would say, thinking or -- and I simply cannot accept this document absolutely as a valid. If you're asking me about disintegration of former Yugoslavia, disintegration started when? That's real question. Secondly, if we are talking about disintegration, we still have, you know, federal bodies dealing with even complex, quite complex situation in former Yugoslavia, and dealing practically not in 1990s when political situation was, I would say, political [indiscernible], but rather would say dealing with complexity in former Yugoslavia since 1981 when first crisis started from Kosovo. And later on, and later on. So that is my response.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I just want to ask you about one other thing in relation to this document. Please, can we look at the third page in English. And I think in B/C/S, it's also -- yes, third page as well. We see in -- in the middle of the first paragraph, and I think this should give us the date even more, a large number of JNA units relocated from Slovenia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Presenting a strong factor of stability. Now when did the JNA pull out of Slovenia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I think it started when Slovenian government announced independency.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you give us a date.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, don't worry, I don't want to waste time.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I can give you some my writing about -- from my book to tell you. But I don't remember exactly the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry about that. But anyhow, what I want to ask you about is this: "With regard to that, the present state of security of the Serbian people in BH shall, to a large extent, continue to depend on a successful collaboration between the MUP and the JNA, particularly in those municipalities where the Serbian people are a minority. Presently the security and protection of the Serbian people can be enhanced and improved through certain organisational changes within the MUP without fully decentralising it." Now, first of all, had you heard opinions like this being expressed?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Not in particular from anybody. And I, again, telling you I don't know whose opinion was implemented in this paper. If you're asking me personally, I would say that relocation of JNA from Slovenia and Croatia wasn't factor of stability for Bosnia. Rather, would say it was factor of instability in Bosnia. I'm saying this -- when you see, you know, JNA coming from Croatia and Slovenia, you have atmosphere between people of insecurity, of something forthcoming that nobody wanted to see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. So, I mean, had you heard anybody express the view within your ministry?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Not at all. And in particular, look, saying here, The Serbian people are a minority.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, it's saying -- sorry, sir. It's saying that the current safety of the Serbian people in municipalities where they are minority - not over all, but in municipalities - depends on cooperation between the MUP and the JNA. Is that something you had heard expressed by --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- any of your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: No. Not by my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then the next paragraph, which starts: "In conditions of latent danger ..." Yes. We see the fifth sentence down: "The MUP must rely on the JNA and work in concert with it. Decentralisation of internal affairs is not in the interest of safety of the Serbian people, because this decentralisation implies forming internal affairs organs only in municipalities with a Serbian majority." Now, had -- did you, during the period of 1991, hear any discussion of the idea of decentralising the MUP?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Not really. And I can accept that decentralisation of [indiscernible] is not only in the interests of safety of entire Bosnia and Herzegovina people, not only Serbian people. That is my -- my opinion. Secondly, our ministry had very, very close, I would say, relationship with JNA in case regarding equipment, in case of forming mutual check-points in former Bosnia, to prevent and to do everything possible practically to prevent eventually conflict in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So do I take that all the ideas expressed in this paper, including the conclusions, the proposals that there should be -- if we go to the -- I suppose we better have a look at it. It's page 5 in English, I think, and page -- sorry, it's page -- page 4 in English, probably the fifth page then. And in the B/C/S, it's page 5. Oh, no, yes, I'm sorry, I want to go on a bit further. Sorry, it's my fault. It's this bit. No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we please go to the bottom of that page in English. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay, This is the conclusions there -- and I don't know whether you have got it up in the B/C/S language, I don't think you have. But is effectively that there should be - well, we can see - a separate Serbian MUP. Did you ever hear that being discussed?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. From about when?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Well, in early January, in 1991, if I remember well, it was meeting in Lisbon, on the governing Mr. Cutileiro --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, that's not my --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: And I heard from my resources that Alija Izetbegovic and Dr. Karadzic proposed to Mr. Cutileiro to divide interior ministry on national basis forming committee of nine members who will deal with separate interior ministries in Bosnia-Herzegovina. As I received, you know, information from my sources, I ask, on the following day, on the prime minister cabinet, because two members of the prime minister cabinet being present there, Branko Djeric, who came later, first, president of Republika Srpska prime minister, and Rusmir Mahmutcehajic. And I ask our prime minister before dealing with other issues on the meeting, to explain on which authority they being present there and, you know, not acting regarding interior ministry as members of prime minister cabinet. I was heavily, I would say, criticised by prime minister, saying that I'm trying to -- I would say, intercept or follow or [indiscernible] or whatever, about his cabinet members. And we didn't have a meeting, cabinet meeting. He called President Izetbegovic, and we had a meeting with Presidency. And I asked also -- Dr. Karadzic wasn't present on that meeting, and I asked Mr. Izetbegovic as president of Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina to explain to -- and publicly announced on TV or on General Assembly initiative for two political leaders in front of international negotiation for peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina proposal to divide interior ministry on national basis. Again, of course, being strongly criticised at the time, you know, tried to control political leaders and members of Presidency, wasn't my intention, was my role. So if you are asking me about initiative, it was proposed early January in 1991 during meeting with Mr. Cutileiro in Lisbon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So I don't think there is any dispute that you're a year out. It was 1992. So --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: 1992, sorry, you're right, sorry, I apologise. Yes, early in January 1992, sorry, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before I ask you some further questions --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I obviously can't get the document exhibited, admitted as exhibit, but I would ask it be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise. Your Honours, to correct the transcript, the documents, the charts admitted previously, would be Exhibits P873 through Exhibit P881, and 65 ter number 23 will become Exhibit P882, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before January 1992 had you heard about proposals to create a separate -- a separate Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That was the first you heard of it?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, and in connection with something that you said earlier, to have a look at document 2702.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, did somebody catch that? Oh, right. We seem to be stuck.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I don't think I want to waste time on this. I mean, if we can't get it up, we can't get it up. We'll come back to it. Is it just that document or all documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand the system has crashed. And as I'm now going to be going through documents with the witness, I think we may have to take an early adjournment. He can't get this document off and anything else up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The document I asked to have put up was 2702.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Korner, is it a very large document?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, two pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I gather that the Gods of technology have determined that we take an adjournment to have this matter looked at. I suppose the Registry will notify us when we can resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It is proposed that we take the normal break now and resume in 20 minutes, and then sit to the ordinary time that we rise for the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I gather -- sorry. Can I just mention one thing. I know you've got -- there's a matter you want to deal with. The technical problems have been resolved. But, Your Honour, I understand that effectively there may be a problem with the fact that Mr. Zepinic is choosing to go speak English. Whilst his English is, of course, very fluent, occasionally he is quite difficult to understand by the interpreters, and there has been problems with Mr. Cvijetic actually getting a proper translation, not to mention the problem that I'm doing what everyone else normally does, which is starting my question too soon. And we wondered whether Your Honours would care to ask him if he would kind enough to speak in the Serbian language. I think that may help everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We actually considered it, but thought that since he chose himself to speak English, we would just let him continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, But I think it is causing problems with the transcript and the interpreters. And Mr. Cvijetic is going to cross-examine, so it is obviously important that he hears everything that is said, or gets translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I add it is important for the clients for our -- for the accused also to hear the testimony in the language that they understand. Your Honours, there is just one matter I need to raise. On page 47, line 21 to 24 of today's transcript, the witness I understood as saying that he needed to check his book in order to provide a date for a certain answer that Ms. Korner was asking him. Now, we checked with our friends from the Prosecutor's side, and they are not aware of existence of any book written by this witness, and therefore this book was not disclosed as they were not aware of it. So I don't know what is -- what is the proper way -- I was -- I was kind of hoping to ask the Trial Chamber to clarify the situation. We don't know whether the witness actually wrote the book or he is -- he is talking about his notes, maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he said book. The transcript said b-o-o-n-g. But he meant book, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Perhaps Ms. Korner can ask him to clarify it. But I would have thought his notebook, but we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It was just my understanding that he referred to his book, and he wanted to take it out of his attache case, so we would just need the clarification. And if is a book, it should be disclosed to us, obviously. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours will appreciate we have had limited contact with him. And I don't think it occurred to anybody ask him whether he had actually written a book about these events, so that's why this has happened. But I'm certainly prepared to ask him about the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zepinic, before you continue, we know that you have expressed a preference to testify in English. However, there are certain difficulties not unsurmountable which this -- this raises for both sides, and we are wondering whether it is a decision that you would care to reconsider. It seems to counsel on both sides and to the Chamber that it may be simpler if you were to speak in what was originally your native language. We appreciate your facility --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No problem at all, absolutely. Why didn't say it before. That's fine. Your Honour, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Zepinic, can I, just before we look at this document which we tried to get up last time, ask you -- you mentioned a book that you had written earlier. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you've got it with you, have you?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure, to be honest. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. The request has been, I am afraid, that nobody seems to have appreciated that you had written a book, whether you would have any objection -- is it in English or in -- in Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my book that I published a long time ago, in 1985, entitled: "Do you smoke?" But, at the moment I am working on a book, actually my biography and the events that took place at the time. This particular book was written a long, long time ago. I have been fighting smoking for a long time, and, for that reason, I wrote the book.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is clearly one I ought to read then. However, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: [In English] I give you as a present. It is no problem at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll leave that, and the Defence can ask you anything else they want to ask but that. Can we now look at the document, please. This document, as we can see is the SDS inviting following members of the SDS party employed in the government. And if we look at number 10 your name appears, and indeed on the original, there seems to be some ticks, but --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Firstly did you ever receive an invitation to attend sessions of the SDS Deputies Club?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: As I said, I attended meetings of the Deputies Club, not only of the SDS but also the Serbian Democratic Party and the HDZ. When security issues were on the agenda, the security issues in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is. The policy was that parties may invite certain members that would appear on behalf of the party and have undertaken certain obligations in different ministries and other republican organs. This is probably a list of the Serbian Democratic Party. I don't know the date, but by looking at it, it contains all of us that were in one way or another involved or appointed to various ministries and other institutions that were at the level of the government, the parliament, or the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It says that the following, including you, although in the English version your name has been misspelt, members of the SDS. I think you told us earlier you weren't a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe there is a mistake in translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, really?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian version does not say ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I agree with you. In the English version, it says that the following members of the Serbian Democratic Party shall be invited. But in the original it says, cadres that work in the ministries and other republic organisations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I am grateful Mr. Zecevic for your intervention. Your Honours, could that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P883, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to move to looking at some of the events in 1991 through some of the intercepts which you have had a chance to listen to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have up on the screen, please -- sorry. It's one of the ones Your Honours referred to. It's 10249. Your Honours, may I ask at this stage, because this shows that Mr. Zepinic was a party to this call, whether Your Honours want it played or whether I can simply lead him on the basis that he has identified the voices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You may lead him, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is one of the ones you listened to. And the other person on the phone is Rajko Dukic. Djukic or Dukic?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Dukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Dukic. Can you tell us who he was, at this stage?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Rajko Dukic was in charge in the Serbian Democratic Party, actually he was the chairman of the executive committee, and he was in charge for personnel affairs within the party.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this phone call is you to him, and you're complaining about Biljana Plavsic who was going to come over to the Ministry of Interior. First of all, this is March 1991. Can you remember - very briefly - what this was about. If you can't, say so straight away.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I remember very well what happened here. I had been informed that barricades had been erected in Sarajevo. This information came from Mr. Dukic at around 7.00 p.m. on the 1st of March, 1992. I immediately went to the ministry, my ministry. There were problems given that the barricades had already been set up in the city. I went to the office. I tried to get in touch with members of the Presidency in the hope that this issue can be resolved. Of all members of the Presidency, Biljana Plavsic was the only one who responded to my call that I made after I visited certain points and barricades in Sarajevo and that was sometime after midnight, I would say, between 1.00 and 2.00 in the morning. Mr. Izetbegovic didn't show any interest at all for me to meet him either in the Presidency or in the MUP building in order to solve this problem because he thought that was exclusively the matter for the security organs. I didn't manage to locate other members of the Presidency, because, Krajisnik, Koljevic, and Karadzic were not in Sarajevo but were in Belgrade attending a meeting. Mr. Plavsic responded and said that she would come to the ministry building, in order to try to solve this in a peaceful way. However, later, in a conversation with Dukic, I learned that she insisted that General Kukanjac be involved in that as well, who was the commander of the 5th Army in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I believe that any involvement of the army in resolving the problem of barricades in Sarajevo would be totally counter-productive, that that would cause an even grater chaos and probably direct armed conflicts at the barricades that had been erected by the Muslim forces. And that probably that would cause escalation of conflicts not only in Sarajevo, but probably in other towns in Bosnia-Herzegovina. My opinion was that the barricades have to be resolved through political agreements between the nationalist party, primarily I referred to the SDA and the SDS, because the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Party, didn't have a single barricade set up by their members. As I said, the barricades were erected on behalf of the political parties and on nationalist basis; therefore, I thought that relevant political figures should be involved in solving this situation. I was extremely, so to say, disappointed by the fact that members of the Presidency didn't think that it was necessary for them to get involved. And I said with the exception of Mrs. Plavsic. Only in the morning at around 7.00, we finally had a meeting in the Presidency which was attended by Mr. Izetbegovic, Ganic, and other members of the Presidency, except Professor Koljevic who was absent. At this meeting, I took the opportunity to tell them that this kind of irresponsible conduct in such a situation, which unfortunately still remained unsolved because the barricades remained in place for a long time, particularly the conduct of Mr. Ganic who on behalf of the Presidency was appointed as a person in charge of resolving possible crises in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I thought that this extremely critical and chaotic situation necessitated an involvement of all political factors in order to find a political solution. And that this, in any way, should be resolved by -- shouldn't be resolved by involving the army or any other armed force, which later proved to be the case. So Dukic as the only one in the SDS party who was present there was the one who I asked to call and to invite Mrs. Plavsic. I expected her to come together with Mr. Izetbegovic so that we could solve this problems without involving the army and General Kukanjac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. It looks like -- thank you very much for that explanation. Sorry, I was going to chronologically. But from what you say, the date, 1991, is an error, and it should read 1992. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry about that because --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, having said that, may it be admitted and marked, please. It's on the list of the ones that you admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P884, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. In that case, I need to take you -- I'm sorry, I need to ask you about an earlier intercept in 1991. Could we have up on the screen, please, 1027. 1024, I beg your pardon. 1024.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, this is an intercept you listened to. Is that right, Dr. Zepinic? And you were able to identify your voice and of that Radovan Karadzic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about some of the content. Karadzic was asking you on the first page about you being with Rajko. Do you know who he was referring to there?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I believe that he was referring to Rajko Dukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And there's a conversation -- there's a question from Karadzic. Has he been stopped, Tomo? And you ask which?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we go to the next page in English, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the response is: Kovac. Can you remember now what the problem was -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: This was probably Tomo Kovac who was the commander of the public security station at Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And do you know what the problem was that required him to be stopped?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: [In English] I can't remember -- sorry. [Interpretation] I cannot remember because I have seen a lot of material to that effect. But if you show me how this conversation went on, maybe I can tell you what we talked about and why Tomo Kovac was the subject of this conversation between Mr. Karadzic and myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It may be the next part. Because Karadzic goes on say there are terrible complaints about him. And then changes the subject, Please tell me, what happened with the Special Police unit. The command has changed there, hasn't it? In about May of 1991 was there a -- a change notice command of the Special Police unit?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: No. Throughout the whole period, when I assumed my position, the commander of the special unit was Dragan Vikic. There were pressures from all three nationalist parties for Dragan Vikic to be replaced and dismissed. There was also pressure relating to who should be given this position on the level of nationality, when it came to who should command the special unit. However, we did not replace Dragan Vikic. We even reinforced by well-trained personnel who were able to lead the unit. So apart from these personnel changes, basically, the commander remained in place, and that was the commander who discharged his duties even before we assumed our position. Then Karadzic insisted that we try to find a way for it to be given to a Serb. On the other hand, Izetbegovic insisted on this position to be given to a Muslim. But since the two of them couldn't reach agreement who should be the commander, the best possible solution was to retain the professional who had been at the head of this unit for years without any problems. We tried the best we could for members of this unit to be corresponding to the national composition of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm sorry, the wrong page is up on the screen in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have the second page. Not the third, which is up at the moment. Yeah. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because later down that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Further on, I don't know, in B/C/S, you need the -- the second page. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You go on to say that, We will try to have it connected with the minister exclusively. And Karadzic queries that. And you say: The minister or his deputy. And then Karadzic says: All right, but it still has to have a commander. So was there a discussion at that stage going on about the whole set-up of the special unit with Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: There was no discussion about how it was composed. Dr. Karadzic wanted, if possible, the commander to be a Serb. As I already explained, we changed the document on the basis of which the special unit can be engaged in an action, and that this could not, under any circumstances, be done without co-signature of two of us and our consent. So, in that sense, the commander of this unit couldn't be in a situation and wouldn't dare activate or use the unit or part of the unit without the signatures and the consent of the two of us. It would have been totally irrelevant whether the commander of the Special Police unit was Chinese or an Indian or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: If he was a professional and if he did his job well, and if he obeyed orders signed by the two of us, then it was totally irrelevant what his descent was. For that reason, I didn't accept Dr. Karadzic's suggestion for the commander to be replaced.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I want to ask you -- because there is a lot of discussion about various personnel, but I want it ask you about one other thing in this intercept.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we go in the English to the fifth page. And in the B/C/S, to the fourth. And we need to scroll up, please, in the English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There's a discussion about what ethnicity or nationality people belong to. And then Karadzic says -- there's going to be a meeting. And there's -- something about a group that is against Mico, and you say: Yes And I told them not to give us any crap; we know exactly what we are doing. Besides, Mico can't, and this should be your argument as well. Mico can't do it because we would lose a Member of Parliament. If he were in the Council of Citizens, he would not -- he would be able to, because he would leave the ... position, be next off the list, et cetera, et cetera. Do you know who is he referring to there?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I suppose that he is talking about Mr. Stanisic here. There was a -- an initiative for Mr. Stanisic to be appointed chief of the CSB Sarajevo. There was equally other initiatives coming from some members of the SDS, not to nominate him on behave of the SDS for that position. Whether he was a member of the deputies club of the Serbian Democratic Party, I don't know, and I have no documents relating to that. But according to our rule books, members of the MUP were allowed to be members of political parties, but there had to leave aside their political affiliations and give precedence to their professional duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. That that's all I asked. May that be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P885, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look very quickly please at 3028.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the same day as the previous conversation. Again, with you and Dr. Karadzic. And all I want to ask you about is this. Karadzic there is saying to you, and if we look at the bottom of the page in English -- yes. Can you please keep Kovac in Ilidza. Does that ring any bells as to what the problem was with Kovac?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: The problem with Kovac was that he was the commander of the police station at Ilidza even before we assumed our positions. In the personnel division of jobs between the political parties, this particular job was allocated to the Serb, but there was some objections and Mr. Stanisic would remember that in conversation between him and Mr. Tinta [phoen], it was threatened that 10.000 demonstrators would appear in Vogosca if Kovac remained commander of the police station at Ilidza. Kovac fulfilled all the legal regulations according to our rules to carry out this duty, and he was fully qualified for that. Political arguments that he was unsuitable because of his political affiliation was something that I couldn't accept as a criterion for appointments to any position whatsoever for a very simple reason, that, by -- that I thought one should insist that everyone should carry out their job professionally. In many conversations with our political leaders, I expressed my readiness to have in my ministry 11.000 members of the MUP of one single ethnicity, provided that they carry out their duties in a professional manner. And, on that basis, I could guarantee them that jobs would be done professionally. So these division along ethnic lines within the ministry was an insane idea from whoever it came from. And I was very much opposed to it, especially when it came to executive positions, who primarily had the duty of performing their job in a professional way and to serve as a role model and convey this professionalism to their subordinates. If any of the executives in the Ministry of the Interior showed his exclusive party affiliation, I thought that those who were under him were justified in questioning his professionalism and professionalism of all other executive officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P886, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you look, please, now at -- again, it is a conversation the same day, 3360, but not between you and Mr. Karadzic, so -- I just want to ask you about the content. Right. You listened to this one. Were you able to identify, even though you weren't present at this, the voices on the tape? Leaving aside, Mrs. Karadzic, the former Mrs. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Karadzic, yes, Ljilja. I recognised Ljilja's voice, too, although we didn't speak much either over the phone or in person. And as far as Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Zupljanin are concerned, I recognised their voices for the simple reason that we had a great many conversations on the phone and we also met often in person. So it was no problem for me to recognise a conversation between the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. At the bottom of the page in English - yeah - Mr. Zupljanin is saying to Karadzic that: "A dispatch had arrived from the federal SUP, and I talked with the deputy Vito. He assigned me to go and pick them up at 10.00 tomorrow morning and to make the exchange." Is that a reference to you, or to somebody else?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please have the tab number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He probably meant me because I know this case. It would -- asked by the federal MUP, we made an assessment, because three officers of the federal MUP had been illegally detained in Kninska Krajina. And these guys who were from the federal MUP had to be taken over from Babic. And I asked to resolve the issue in a couple of phone calls with Milan Babic. There was were some delays, I can't really remember why, but I got really mad, and I said, Okay, if you don't agree, then we'll send our special unit forces from Banja Luka to liberate them. And I informed Mr. Zupljanin, because that was part of his remit as the nearest SJB to the Kninska Krajina, and told him to go there with a group of his staff and accept these three persons from Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You said, first of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before you continue, Ms. Korner, I don't know if they still need it, but before the witness had started the answer, the interpreters had asked for the tab number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The tab number? Oh, I see, I didn't catch that. It's tab number 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said, first of all, that it was part of his remit as the nearest SJB. Do you mean SJB or CSB?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Speaking about such things, it was natural for the CSB to take care of them. That is, the chief of the CSB would -- the forces that -- that were specialised on that, rather than the nearest station which was Grahovo, if I remember well. But the Banja Luka centre was closest, so it was only natural for them to do it, if that had happened at Trogir, then the nearest CSB would have been Mostar. Or in the case of Slavonski Brod, then the CSB of Tuzla would have been closest. So it all depended on where the event had happened. I remember this case. I know that Zupljanin went there with a group of his co-workers and that it was taken care of in a way which did not cause unnecessary subsequent complications when it comes to the relations between the security forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina and those of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. There are just two other matters I want to ask you about in connection with in intercept.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If one looks at the third page in English, and it's -- I seem to have failed to mark it in B/C/S. It's also the third page in the B/C/S. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stojan Zupljanin says in the middle of the English page, and I hope it is in that page somewhere, but that Avdo Hebib is trying to go down there with him. Karadzic asks why, or effectively. And he says, I don't know what the devil's up. I told Vito as well not to send him. No way, Vito, let him be captured and then exchanged for Vojkovac. Again, is he talking about you there?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In fairness to the witness I don't believe that the Serbian version corresponds to the English in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... citing from Ms. Korner is not on the -- on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry about this, Your Honours. I thought I had marked up all the B/C/S, but obviously I failed to do it in this case. Ah, it's on page -- got it. The fourth page in the Serbian language. Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you remember Zupljanin saying something to you about not sending Avdo Hebib?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that any mention was made of Avdo Hebib, who was assistant for police, to act as a mediator in this liberation action with Kninska Krajina or, rather, release action. So I cannot confirm that. And I don't see a reason why Avdo Hebib, with regard to his position, should not do the job, although he is of a different ethnicity. So if his engagement had been sought for, why not?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The next question is this, leaving aside whether you remember this, was Zupljanin in the habit of, as it were, giving you orders, it looks like, if that's the right way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Zupljanin issued orders to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you saying I told Vito as well not to send him. I don't mean orders in the proper sense. Clearly the chain of command was you, and then he was below. But was he somebody who would, can I put it this way then, put his point of view forcefully to you?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, regardless of my position it was always my custom to consult not only the chiefs of the centres or the chiefs of the police stations but maybe even with regular police officers. If that would enable me to get information or find the best possible solution. I repeat that I don't remember this particular incident, so I cannot directly answer your question. But if, for any reason, Stojan Zupljanin thought that the appearance of Avdo Hebib would have been counter-productive with regard to completing the job which could have been done by the CSB of Banja Luka, I would have accepted that. The same way as I would have accepted Zupljanin's insistence that Avdo Hebib come on the occasion of the conflict at Bosanska Krupa, if I remember probably. I always made an effort to respect my co-workers. Whether they respected me in turn is for them to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] And the final matter on this particular intercept that I want to ask you about is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The final matter I want to ask you about on this intercept is on the last -- sorry, the fourth page of the English. And I hope on the fifth page -- maybe the fourth page of the B/C/S. Sorry. It's the -- it's the fourth page of the B/C/S, at the bottom, I think. Zupljanin says to Dr. Karadzic: "Mr. Karadzic, I felt it was necessary to inform you ..." And Karadzic replies: "Oh, thank you very much. It's not easy for you. Be strong." First question: Were you aware that Stojan Zupljanin would be effectively ringing Karadzic and going over your head?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that he spoke with Mr. Karadzic about this case. This was an activity, in my opinion, of which I wouldn't have informed Karadzic or any other politician. Because it was a professional task for the CSB, which did what was demanded of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, in line with the ruling, may I just have this marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P887 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like now to ask you to look, please, at a document around this period -- if I can find my list. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 2582, please, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 16th of May of 1991. It's a decision, apparently signed by Mr. Delimustafic, appointing Mico Stanisic as the secretary of the Sarajevo SUP. Were you aware of -- of this official decision?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Just a correction. The signature is mine, rather than Delimustafic's. But each decision of appointment bore the name of the minister. So, officially, I appointed Mico Stanisic to his position of secretary of the SUP of Sarajevo, and as -- and naturally this document is known to me. If I may just add a comment with regard to this appointment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: With your leave, Your Honours, before Mico Stanisic Mr. Kemo Sabovic was in this position who was a professional, Mico knows him. He had been a police inspector for a long time, and he was a top professional. However, the SDA didn't think him suitable, and Izetbegovic insisted several times that Kemo Sabovic be replaced from the position of head or, rather, secretary of the SUP of Sarajevo. I did not accept the reasoning given, because I considered Mr. Sabovic's qualifications and experience as well as professionalism merit his -- him remaining in that position. But that was probably due to the rivalry of the political leaders Karadzic and Izetbegovic, and the SDA would then cede to the SDS this position. I don't know which the conditions were, which conditions were attached to that. And I was duty-bound to appoint a Serb to the position of secretary of the SUP of Sarajevo. The SDS proposed several candidates, by Mico Stanisic met all the criteria, and the -- as set out in the regulations. And so he met all the conditions to be appointed to this position, and I indeed appointed him. This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P888.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before we come to the next document, in terms of time, can we go back, please, to some of the intercepts that you listened to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we go, please, to 17th of June; in fact, the same day as this. It's document number 1027, please; tab 8 for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could we have a 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought I said it. 1027.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which is you and again Mr. Karadzic -- sorry, I say it was the same day, it's [indiscernible]. We're moving into June, and I think you were again able to identify your voice and that of Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognised both voices.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, here, there's -- there's a long discussion which starts on that very -- we can see, which is about the minister of the interior procuring anti-armour weapons. And you explain that -- it's not your decision. It's -- I'm sorry. It is determined by the army. And there's a long discussion about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then could we go, please, in English to the fifth page. And in the B/C/S, to the fourth page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the middle of the page, Karadzic -- Dr. Karadzic is asking about the staff of the MUP. And then Draskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then at the bottom of the page, in English, please, scroll up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Look please, tonight I need very clear information. I have negotiations with Izetbegovic tomorrow at 9.00. At 10.00 we have the assembly. There's no way that an appointment" --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page, please, in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "... or a change in personnel could happen without the approval of the SDS. Anything that concerns nominations an appointments. Not a single situation concerning staff." We see a number of conversations where he is effectively cross-examining you about what's happening. And here he makes it absolutely plain, according to him, that there can be no appointments without the approval of the SDS. Was that a view that he expressed on more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: If I may correct you in your introduction into this document where you called him a minister. Or, rather, when you said that the minister had ordered anti-armour weapons. It was actually the ministry based on the assessment that we should equip ourselves as well we could to keep peace and order in Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, no such weapons could be bought without the approval of the JNA in accordance with the then law. We had reason to arm ourselves well, to prevent the break-up of Yugoslavia. However, the political leaders that out from our minister, and then interventions ensued, to check whether that was correct or not. You will have been able to tell that I evaded giving Mr. Karadzic a clear answer. About personnel, or cadres, Karadzic insisted that no -- nobody could be appoint without the approval of the SDS. That was his opinion, just as it was the opinion of the two other political leaders to whom -- or, rather, with which opinion I didn't agree. Because it was my idea and wish, and it was my effort to appoint a professional to any position. I didn't think it a great problem for any political party to find a professional from the ranks of their own ethnicity. But I didn't need a loyal party member of any ethnic party in my ministry. I needed people who would go about their duties in a professional fashion for the benefit of all inhabitants of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This conversation between me and Mr. Radovan Karadzic, and you will probably have recordings of my conversations with Mr. Izetbegovic in which I insisted very energetically and I even invited SDA leaders to my office to ask them whether it was in the interest of any ethnic party to insist that loyal party members be appointed to executive positions if those members had criminal files or police files. And I wanted those political leaders to clearly say so at their assemblies. So this was my opposition to it be to the appointment of party cadres rather than to professionals to positions in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, you say you wanted those political leaders to clearly say so at their assemblies. In June of 1991 there was just the one assembly wasn't there, of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, a General Assembly; I'm talking about a General Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, could that admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P889, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want you to look now again at a conversation that you weren't a party to but where you appear to get a mention? Could we have up -- it's the same day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And could we have up, please, number 2669. Oh, tab 9, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, it is a conversation that you listened to. Were you able to identify the voices of Biljana Plavsic and Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karadzic and Ms. Plavsic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. In the middle of the first page, you say -- he -- Karadzic -- sorry, Biljana Plavsic is saying that Dukic was here, and then Neskovic. "They're all complaining bitterly that I should tell you about the MUP. Rajko's not letting anyone say a thing against Zepinic, and everyone else is saying that it's awful how susceptible to the influence of these people." This is connected with barricades that have been erected in, apparently, in Sokolac. Were aware of people making complaints about you, and Rajko protecting you, Rajko Dukic?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I don't know if Rajko Dukic protected me. If he did, I'm grateful to him. This is the first time I hear of it. But this is -- this is a criticism to my opposition to the efforts of the ethnic parties, but I was criticised by everybody. And I didn't want to give in to this pressure, The more so since on some occasions I offered my resignation to the political leaders, the president of the assembly, the prime minister, the president of the Presidency, if they thought that I was an opponent to the political parties. The concrete mention of Mr. Neskovic is because I replaced him for justified reasons, and Mr. Karadzic accepted that, because he knew my reasons. And he didn't deem it necessary to discuss that at all. Why Mr. Plavsic [as interpreted] had this conversation with Mr. Karadzic, I don't know. It's a fact that on several occasions we had some contradictory reports at the Security Council -- at Security Council meetings of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and because there had been attempts to politicise the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: That I was criticised from this side and the other and the third, well, what can you do?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There is one other matter here that is dealt with here by Mrs. Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look, please, at page 3 of the English and page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic is saying: "He is one of the three MUP guys. "Put pressure on him for that. "They tricked him or he made a deal," and that's another matter. "Yes, all right." And then Radovan Karadzic is saying: "Put a lot of pressure on; we mustn't let them in in any way." This appears to be in connection with the council in the MUP. But did Mrs. Plavsic put pressure on you to do anything?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Well, look, Mrs. Plavsic even asked the Federal Secretariat for National Defence on behalf of the committee for the protection of the constitutional order of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is due to criminal proceedings against him which is total unlawful and illegal. As for her role as member of the Presidency, there is no disputes about that. This was reflected throughout the whole period that I was in power. The fact that I didn't believe that the three members of the MUP taken over by Mr. Zupljanin from Knin and solved this problem, somebody should gain some political points for any political party. And for that reason, I think that this was done at my request, or, rather, the ministry's requests, sent to the Banja Luka CSB, in a professional and expert manner, without giving any political credibility to any political party because I thought that to be totally inappropriate, that anyone should gain some political points for doing a professional job.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that just be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What it says here, put pressure on him, you know, that was their style. But what can you do?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P890, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when you say that was their style, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: You see, the political style of all the three political parties and the three political leaders was to politicise as much as possible the MUP. That is to say to exert direct pressure on executives within the MUP, in order to give preference to one or the other party, particularly when it came to the appointment of specific executive officers. I have to tell that you we had tremendous problems not only with the SDS but also with the remaining two parties. It often happened that they with a nominate a candidate that didn't fulfil absolutely a single requirement according to the rule on internal organisation. He lacked -- he or she lacked qualification, lacked any experience to make them a candidate who was appropriate for the proposed job, and the worse thing was that often it happened that such a candidate who was proposed on a political basis and is loyal to political party had a criminal record. So imagine if you appoint someone who did time for a few months for some criminal offences to the position of a commander or police station. I simply couldn't and wouldn't accept such policies. And I don't think that anyone should accept that, if we want to have professionalism. However, since this concept of mine didn't suit our political leaders was not my problem. They had a problem with me. But that was the time it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we move then, please, to the next document, which is tab 10 for the interpreters. And it's 3030.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, this is a conversation with Radovan Karadzic, and originally it was put "unidentified male." But if we looked at the last page, it -- it says it was you. And are you able to confirm having listened to this conversation -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't -- because of the time I don't want to spend any more time. Can I simply ask that it be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P891.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want you to look next, please, at the report of the 24th of June. And that is 65 ter 8. I think this is a report that you were aware of at the time headed: On activities relating to changes in senior officers at the Ministry of Interior and the need to bring the ethnic structure of employees more into line with the ethnic structure of the population. The report is dated but not actually, I think, signed by anyone. Do you know who wrote the report?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: This is information that the Ministry of the Interior sent to the government, to the Presidency, and the parliament at the request of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina relating to bringing into line the national structure of the staff with the national structure of the population. I cannot remember all the details, but this information depicts the entire structure of the MUP, including the State Security Service. Based on ethnicity, age, and other criteria that were asked of us to provide. According to this material, if I remember correctly, a significant percentage of members of the MUP, including myself, declare themselves Yugoslavs, which the national leaders extremely resented, because they thought that those who belonged to this particular ethnic group should be appointed on the principle that the national ethnicity of the ministry should reflect the national composition of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In political terms, can I accept that, but I couldn't accept any discussion about what we were going to do with around 650 people, members of the staff, who did not want to declare their ethnicity for any reason. We also had a certain disproportion in the MUP in comparison to the national composition of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I have to say that as far as the Serbs are concerned, the percentage of the staff was higher than the percentage of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina. But, as I said, I abided by the principle to speak only about professionalism, and I think this is at this Presidency meeting that I presented this information, and at this meeting I said that I wouldn't mind having a single ethnicity in my ministry providing they all do their job in a professional way and that by that, I would guarantee them that the ministry would fulfil all its obligations in a professional manner, as required by the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P892, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look, please, at a conversation with you, Mandic, and Karadzic together, on 24th June; tab 13, 65 ter number 1034. This is a very long conversation. It starts off with you, and then Mandic -- you and Karadzic, and then Mandic and Karadzic have a talk. I just want to ask you about one matter in this. First of all, I think you have identified your voice, that of Mandic and that of Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Karadzic says at the bottom of page one in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Please if we move to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "I was in Nevesinje and Visegrad," and then goes on to say, "three guys were severely beaten" --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, can we go to the next page, I think it is, in each. Sorry, I said in each. It's not in English. Can we have the next page in B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you talk about a Working Group led by -- and Karadzic says: "I said they should not, by any means, take anywhere down there any illegal action. Let them be beaten, let them suffer, let" -- something or other else. I don't know what that means. But do you know what that was about?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I don't know specifically which case it was. It has to do with Nevesinje; that's correct. This initiative and this conversation with Mr. Karadzic was unacceptable, given that he wanted to score some political points, and if one cannot do that, then it must be established if any offence was committed on the ground that should be sanctioned under the law. So his saying let them be beaten, let them suffer, was something intended to score political points, in order to create chaos and to instill mistrust, mistrust in the other nationality and in the other national ethnic group, and it was inconsistent with the policy. I cannot say specifically which case he is talking here about. But, as you can see, in a certain way, Mr. Karadzic is defying the fact that I appointed a Working Group that was supposed to find out the reasons and the perpetrators of this incident that is being mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we move, then --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, Your Honour. Can I have that marked admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So marked and admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P893.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to move, please, now into July in the last ten minutes or so of this session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you have a look, please, first of all, at the intercept, which is tab 14, 1413. Right. Conversation, 8th of July between you and Mr. Karadzic. Again, I think you identified the voices. And obviously it has come in the -- the recording started in the middle of the conversation, or after the earlier -- because Karadzic is saying this: "I was with Izetbegovic and Zulfikarpasic last night, and I told them openly we would form a parallel government, we would form a parallel police, if they exclude our people in government, and they will still have to pay for them. We would exclude all our people who are armed. We would form completely a parallel state if you continue to fuck us around, and he only stared at me and winked because he knew we would do it." Now, the first thing is, could you tell the Trial Chamber who Zulfikarpasic was?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Abdil Zulfikarpasic was the founder of the SDA party. Later on, he was joined by Alija Izetbegovic. Due to some political reasons and Alija Izetbegovic's being a hard-liner, they went their separate ways. Zulfikarpasic established a Bosnia party that had one or two seats in the parliament, but they remained in coalition with the SDA. So this meeting, whether this meeting actually happened between Karadzic, Zulfikarpasic, and Izetbegovic, and this initiative to create parallel state and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his first sentence. He is speaking too fast. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you can see, they had only one session, and they agreed on only one issue. That is; to keep the power in their hands and to increase the remunerations for the deputies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. The interpreters didn't catch your first sentence about the initiative -- I think the initiative to create a parallel state. They have asked to say that you're talking too quickly.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: I will try to slow down as best I can for the Chamber to be able to hear. That way I will take up a little more time than would probably be required to provide a direct answer. The ethnic parties formed a coalition, and that's how power was structured; the assembly, the cabinet, and the Presidency. Any ethnic party -- but, by the way, having mentioned Mr. Zulfikarpasic and his having -- his party having one or two sets in parliament, and Mr. Filipovic was there on behalf of the Bosnian party, and with the SDS, there was the SPO from Nevesinje with one or two Members of parliament, I'm not sure, I'm sorry. And only due to -- or owing to that coalition did the ethnic party manage to cross the threshold of 50 per cent and establish institutions of power. But this threat -- we leave the coalition. Well, why didn't they? If any of these parties had left the coalition, and if there had been another -- if there had been repeated elections, because that was the duty of the political parties if they were unable to come to terms, and obviously they were not able to agree on anything except on remaining in power and raising the remuneration of the Members of the Parliament who were biding their time, wasting money and time. And this threat, we will leave the institutions of power and establish parallel power structures was a justified idea because it actually meant that the ethnic parties had no more power, and Mr. Karadzic and Izetbegovic knew that very well. And that's why they never published the split of the coalition, the break-up of the coalition, because the break-up of the coalition would have meant that they were losing power. [Previous translation continues] [In English] ... to giving me opportunity to talk further or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I mean -- sorry. It is not actually the question I want to ask. I mean, I just asked you to repeat your first sentence. What I want to ask you about is this. You said to us earlier on this afternoon that you hadn't heard about proposed split in the MUP before the Cutileiro discussions in 1992. When you heard Karadzic say this to you, did you take this seriously?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, come on, this was a totally unserious conversation, such as many other conversations in which the nationalist leaders were saying, We have power, We have power, and so on. I am, of course, speaking for myself now and not for the MUP. And at one meeting it was put to me, at a Presidency meeting, in -- with the participation of others, they were saying that we were elected by the people. Is it possible that the Muslims in Foca were unable to elect a better Member of Parliament than Saja [phoen], or the Serbs from Ozren to elect a better -- worse Serb than Nedic? When I had said that, Mr. Krajisnik kept -- shut up, and the never repeated that they were elected by the people. Possibly the people elected the worse deputies to do what they eventually ended up doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I -- sorry. The problem is, is that we do have a limited time, and as I say, it was a simple question, to which the answer is, no, you didn't take it seriously. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: [In English] No, no, no, not -- absolutely. No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, in any event, may that be marked and admitted. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P894, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Can we move, please, to a document -- well, Your Honours, perhaps I can just get the document -- just show the witness. It's -- all right. Document number 12; 65 ter number 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is a letter written by Mr. Zupljanin to Mrs. Plavsic. Firstly, did she ever show you the letter or speak to you about it?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: No, I only saw this letter here at the Tribunal for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. He is complaining in this letter that, on the 22nd of July, 1991, he was at a meeting at the ministry and couldn't believe his eyes when he received a summary of the systemisation of posts. Not the content but the appearance. Apparently it had been printed in green. Now, all I want to ask you is this. Is that right: Was there a change from the colour of correspondence?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: Not only that it was known to me that there was a change in correspondence. Or, rather, I didn't know. Because I saw this only for the first time here. If I may comment, it is unbecoming for a chief of the Security Service to address directly the head of the State Security -- or, rather, the Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: -- for -- and if I had known about this letter, in the position that I was, I would have probably launched disciplinary proceeds against Mr. Zupljanin, and he would be replaced from his position, and which he was at the time, when he drafted this letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So Mr. Zupljanin takes the view that this was a deep-dyed plot by the Muslims to change the colour to green. Was there any decision made that the correspondence should be changed from blue to green?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC
utterances.text: No. Such a decision was never taken. And I am unaware that there was even discussion about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I ask that that probably be marked for identification. I don't think, as the witness says he hasn't seen it before, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P894, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And this is a convenient point to take the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, I understand that the witness has made a request to know whether is he required to come back tomorrow. This is through VWS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Dr. Zepinic, your testimony is still in the process of -- you're still in the process of being examined by the side that called you, as I explained to you at the beginning, and you are not yet released as a witness. You are excused. This is the time at which the Chamber normally rises, and we would resume in this courtroom -- you will escorted for here for 9.00 tomorrow morning. So the Chamber will indicate to you when you are finally released. But, at this moment, you are required to return tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 29th day of January, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.,
